opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the most likely path isn't a single dramatic moment where a system suddenly becomes a drop-in replacement for a person. It's more that we'll see a gradual broadening of the set of tasks these systems can reliably do end to end, until at some point the bundle of tasks that makes up a given job is mostly covered.

Right now a lot of the value from these models comes from helping with discrete, well-scoped pieces of work: drafting some text, writing a function, answering a question. What's missing for real substitution is the ability to operate over long horizons: keeping track of context across days or weeks, recovering from mistakes, figuring out what to do next when the instructions are ambiguous, and coordinating with other people and tools. That's a lot of what we actually pay humans for. It's not just raw knowledge or reasoning on a single problem. It's agency and reliability over extended stretches of work.

So I'd expect the threshold to be crossed when a few things come together. One is continued scaling of compute and training, which has been the dominant driver of capability gains so far and which I expect to keep going for a while. Another is training specifically for agentic, long-horizon tasks, with environments and feedback that reward completing real projects rather than producing plausible-looking outputs. A third is the surrounding infrastructure: memory, tool use, the ability to act in software environments the way a remote worker would.

One useful way to frame it is to ask when an AI system could do the job of a remote worker, someone who interacts with the world mostly through a computer. Once you have that, the economic implications are enormous, because a huge share of cognitive labor fits that description, and you can run many copies of the system in parallel at relatively low cost. That's where I think you get the real shift, not from AI being a better autocomplete but from AI being able to take on whole roles. And because of that parallelism and the potential to reinvest output into more compute and more R&D, I think there's a reasonable case that once we cross that threshold, the effects on growth could be much faster than people intuitively expect.

r001.rationale: The response says systems lack long-horizon agency and reliability, but does not clearly identify frequent human intervention as a barrier to their economic usefulness.

r002.rationale: It says that parallel systems could reinvest their output into more compute and R&D, supporting further improvement.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare median human performance with expert performance.

r004.rationale: It explicitly describes substitution as gradual broadening across tasks rather than a single abrupt moment, as job bundles become covered.

r005.rationale: It predicts potentially faster growth after the threshold, but does not say substitution accelerates as capabilities progress through the range of human performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Tamay Besiroglu: I think the honest answer is that it's less a single threshold and more a gradual process, and it's useful to be precise about what "substitute" means. Right now, AI systems are pretty good at a lot of individual tasks. They can write code, draft documents, summarize papers, answer questions. But a job isn't a task. A job is a bundle of tasks, plus the coordination between them, plus the context you build up over months or years, plus the ability to handle the long tail of weird situations that nobody wrote down in a job description.

So when we think about substitution, the key question is: can a system do the full bundle, reliably, over long time horizons, with the degree of autonomy that would let you actually hand things off? And that's where current systems fall short. They can do a lot of five-minute tasks and a decent number of one-hour tasks, but they struggle with the multi-day or multi-week projects where you need to maintain state, correct your own mistakes, know when to ask for clarification, and so on.

What we've found in our work at Epoch is that the length of tasks AI can complete autonomously has been growing pretty steadily, roughly doubling every several months. If you extrapolate that trend, you get to systems that can handle week-long or month-long projects within a few years. And I think that's where substitution really starts to bite, because at that point the system isn't just augmenting someone, it's effectively doing the work that would otherwise require hiring a person.

The other piece is that this won't happen uniformly. It'll happen first in domains where tasks are well-specified, outputs are easy to verify, and feedback loops are fast. Software engineering is the obvious example, and I think that's partly why we're seeing so much progress there. Then it spreads to adjacent areas: data analysis, parts of research, various kinds of knowledge work. Physical tasks and tasks requiring deep embedding in messy human institutions will lag.

And I'd add one thing: I think people underestimate how much the economic value comes from scale and cost rather than from matching the best human. A system that's roughly as good as a median professional but costs a hundredth as much and can run thousands of instances in parallel is enormously valuable, even if it's not better than the top expert. So substitution doesn't require superhuman capability. It requires adequate capability at dramatically lower cost, and that's something the compute and algorithmic trends are delivering fairly reliably.

r001.rationale: The response says systems struggle with long projects, self-correction, and knowing when to ask for clarification, but does not identify frequent human intervention as a barrier to economic usefulness.

r002.rationale: It predicts growing AI capability and substitution, but does not say that useful AI would stimulate substantial investment in improving it.

r003.rationale: It says median-professional performance could be economically valuable without matching the top expert, but does not say median performance is easy to match while expert performance remains very difficult.

r004.rationale: It explicitly describes substitution as a gradual process rather than a single threshold and explains that jobs combine many tasks and capabilities.

r005.rationale: It describes capability growth and spread across domains, but does not state that substitution could accelerate as AI progresses through the range of human performance.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s likely to happen gradually, and at different times for different kinds of work. Being a useful substitute for a human doesn’t require an AI system to do everything that person can do. It needs to perform some economically valuable set of tasks well enough, at a sufficiently low cost, that it makes sense to delegate those tasks to it.

The important distinction here is between doing well on an isolated task and reliably carrying out a whole job. A system might be very good at writing a piece of code, but still need someone to explain the requirements, check its work, and help when it gets stuck. That can make it a useful tool without making it a substitute for the person using it.

So I would look at how much human supervision these systems require, and how long they can work effectively without intervention. As they become more reliable and able to handle longer sequences of tasks, the amount of work you can delegate to them grows. In some settings, that will mean people become more productive. In others, it will mean that you no longer need a human to perform that particular role. I don’t think there’s necessarily one sharp threshold separating those two outcomes.

r001.rationale: The response says supervision and intervention can prevent a system from replacing a worker, but does not identify this as a barrier for current AI systems.

r002.rationale: It makes no prediction about useful AI stimulating investment in improvements.

r003.rationale: It does not compare matching median human performance with matching expert performance.

r004.rationale: It says substitution will occur gradually across different kinds of work and that there is no single sharp threshold, consistent with human abilities spanning many tasks.

r005.rationale: It discusses greater reliability and longer task sequences, but does not say substitution could accelerate as capabilities progress through the range of human performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s likely to be a gradual process, and it’ll happen at different times for different tasks. Being very capable at a task isn’t quite the same thing as being a useful substitute for a person. You also need the system to be reliable, to fit into the way work is done, and to require sufficiently little supervision that using it actually saves you time and money.

So I’d expect us to first see systems taking over fairly well-defined pieces of work, where you can specify what you want and check whether the result is good. As they become more reliable over longer stretches of work, you can delegate larger bundles of tasks to them. At some point, those bundles start to look like substantial parts of a job.

The important threshold, I think, is when the cost of getting useful work out of the system—including checking it and correcting its mistakes—is lower than the cost of having a human do it. That doesn’t require the AI to do everything a human can do. But substituting for an entire role is a much higher bar than being useful on individual tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says systems need little supervision and that checking or correcting mistakes adds cost, but it does not identify current AI systems as needing frequent human intervention.

r002.rationale: It does not predict that usefulness will stimulate substantial investment in AI.

r003.rationale: It does not compare matching median human performance with matching expert performance.

r004.rationale: It describes substitution as gradual and occurring at different times for different tasks, with a higher bar for substituting for an entire role than for individual tasks.

r005.rationale: It describes delegation expanding as systems become more reliable, but does not say substitution will accelerate through the range of human performance.
